analyses.titolo: Eyes shut. Ears shut. Alone together.
analyses.corpo: S.U.R.E. asks: do you see light "with your closed eyes"? Feel safe "with your closed ears"? A reading: the real danger is a crowd that stops perceiving. "You're dying in silence between slaves'n'Rulers." Connection starts with open senses.
analyses.caption:
Deep sociality, through one song.

S.U.R.E. opens with questions aimed at your senses: "Do you see light with your closed eyes?" "Do you feel safe enough with your closed ears?" "Do you feel like a prophet with your evil tongue?" Read socially, they map how a group breaks down: we stop looking, we stop listening, we start preaching.

Then the picture widens: "An anthill and the Colosseum", people caught "between slaves'n'Rulers", each one "dying in silence" next to the others. Anger is an acid that does more harm to the "vessel in which it is stored" than to anything on which it is poured, a line about how resentment eats the bonds we live inside.

Our reading: the song doesn't say we are doomed. It says connection is a practice. Open your eyes, open your ears, and "such a simple sum" gets simpler.

S.U.R.E. is track 01 on Roadburn Chronicles. Stream it on Spotify (link in bio).

Which lyric made YOU stop and listen?

analyses.corpo: The Sinner lets the crowd's labels, "an enemy of God", "family ruiner", turn into "an enemy of myself". A reading: we inherit our names from the people around us. The answer here is ownership: "Any color you prefer, they're just a part of me."
analyses.caption:
Who gives us our names?

The Sinner opens with a list of verdicts: "a sinner", "an enemy of God", "family ruiner", "a demon of my time". Read through the lens of deep sociality, they are labels handed down by the people around him. By the last verse the voice has adopted them: "an enemy of myself".

The turn comes with "Any color you prefer, they're just a part of me". Not denial, but ownership. He is "the only one awake among my enemies", which is lonely, and the song ends where it started: "Between fog, dust and rivers", a landscape we all cross with other people's eyes on us.

Our reading, not the last word: belonging is not only being accepted, it is deciding what to do with the names others give you.

The Sinner is track 02 on Roadburn Chronicles. Stream it on Spotify (link in bio).

Which label did you have to grow out of?

analyses.titolo: A lonely path, with other people in it
analyses.corpo: Turning Point calls change "a necessary and lonely hard path". Yet the song keeps talking to a "you": "times you killed", "times you hurt". A reading: you turn alone, but the debts, the damage and the dawn are shared with everyone you touched.
analyses.caption:
A lonely path, with other people in it.

Turning Point describes change as "a necessary and lonely hard path". The images are solitary: a broken compass, breath that is poisonous in the greenest meadows, mud that "tastes like the blood". But read the pronouns. The song never stops talking to a "you": "What will you do now?", "But you raised your head", "times you killed" and "times you hurt".

That is the deep-sociality angle: nobody turns in a vacuum. The dawn ("It's finally dawn") arrives after counting what the old road cost the people around us.

Our reading of the lyrics; yours may differ.

Turning Point is track 03 on Roadburn Chronicles. Stream it on Spotify (link in bio).

What was the moment your wind changed?

analyses.corpo: I For An I sets "Careful boy" against "Old one, old one". Each wants the last word, neither listens: "One blind, one deaf". Yet "I need you, I need it!" A reading: conflict can be a bond wearing armor.
analyses.caption:
A conversation where nobody listens.

I For An I sets two voices against each other: "Careful boy" on one side, "Old one, old one, how sad you are" on the other. Each tells the other to know their place. Each insists on the last word. And then the mask slips: "I need you, I need it!"

Read as deep sociality, it is a portrait of conflict as a form of attachment: the two sides are joined by the very thing they argue about. The line that sums it up is "One blind, one deaf". Nobody sees, nobody hears, and still they are locked together.

The exit the singer chooses is a refusal of the assigned role: "I prefer doubt and fear". Not comfortable, but honest.

Our reading only. Track 04 on Roadburn Chronicles. Stream it on Spotify (link in bio).

Who do you argue with because you can't afford to lose them?

analyses.titolo: Grief is a bench you keep talking to
analyses.corpo: Rusty Blues is sung to an absent father: "I sit and I can talk to you". Life walks by, "young folks and families pass by", and the city feels "so empty and strange". A reading: love outlives presence, and a toast keeps the bond alive.
analyses.caption:
Some conversations continue after the goodbye.

Rusty Blues is addressed to a father who is gone. "Your bench ain't empty anymore", the singer says, "young folks and families pass by", but "when night falls and darkness creeps, I sit and I can talk to you". A toast for Father's Day, red sparkling wine, and the promise to tell it all "to you and mama" someday.

Through the deep-sociality lens, this is grief as a relationship rather than an ending. The city feels "so empty and strange" since he left, and the singer keeps looking for him in strangers: "And when I meet some old white-haired man, I hope it's you, I hope I'm wrong". The community keeps walking by; the bond stays at the bench.

Our reading of the lyrics. Track 05 on Roadburn Chronicles. Stream it on Spotify (link in bio).

Who would you still talk to, if you could?

analyses.titolo: The bite that changes who stands close
analyses.corpo: Viper follows a toxin that brings "Isolation, exile". A reading: temptation is rarely solitary, it lives between two people ("My perversion, your innocence"), and it is paid for socially: "hate, regret, side effects". Then: "Now I see their blinded faces."
analyses.caption:
What does a toxin cost you socially?

Viper is a single about a temptation, a substance or a bond that tastes "so sweet" and arrives with a warning: "Isolation, exile" or "hate, regret, side effects". The elements are two people, not one: "My perversion, your innocence".

For deep sociality, the interesting part is the aftermath. Piece by piece the skin is "polluted by sin", and only then: "Now I see their blinded faces, and now I understand their perturbations". The narrator looks at the people around him and finally understands why they flinched.

Our reading: the real bite of the Viper is not the poison, it is how it rearranges who stands close to you.

Viper is track 06 on Roadburn Chronicles. Stream it on Spotify (link in bio).

Ever been on either side of that bite?

analyses.titolo: Chains for the many, defiance for the few
analyses.corpo: In Revenant "Mortals bow their heads" and someone wants to "Tighten chains", leaving "hearts alone". A reading on deep sociality: obedience is a collective act, and so is rising again. "Defiance burns", "But spirit stands tall".
analyses.caption:
Obedience is collective. So is rising again.

Revenant, the single with the official video, paints a scene where "Mortals bow their heads" and someone wants to "Tighten chains, cold". Freedom "fades fast", hope's embers dim, "Leaving hearts alone". Nobody bows by themselves; it takes a crowd.

But the song keeps answering itself: "Defiance burns", "But spirit stands tall", "Taste my blood, rise again". Deep sociality here means the fragile moment when one person refuses and the others notice.

A reading, not a manifesto. Revenant is track 07 on Roadburn Chronicles. Stream it on Spotify (link in bio).

What would it take to make you stand first?

analyses.titolo: The most intimate sentence on the album
analyses.corpo: Dreamer's Sunsets is one line: "Secret dreams, hold my dreams, side by side with you." Deep sociality in a sentence: intimacy is handing someone what you keep hidden and asking them to hold it, together.
analyses.caption:
The shortest lyric on the album says a lot about us.

Dreamer's Sunsets is a single line: "And she said: Secret dreams, hold my dreams, side by side with you". Deep sociality can be that small. Intimacy is not sharing everything, it is trusting someone with what you keep hidden and asking them to hold it, side by side.

The words come back on track 10: "Secret dreams hoping morning comes too soon. Hold my dreams as the night turns into day. Side by side". Same phrases, told from the road at midnight.

This is our reading, and a very open one: the song leaves you room. Track 08 on Roadburn Chronicles. Stream it on Spotify (link in bio).

Who holds your secret dreams?

analyses.corpo: Monsters' Conceal is a breakup told in silence: "In our route there wasn't you and me". A reading on deep sociality: a relationship lives in the "we", and when it thins, "the silence screams too loud". Even then the song asks together: "Are we to blame?"
analyses.caption:
When the "we" disappears, what is left?

Monsters' Conceal is a breakup told without shouting. "No angry cries", just "the hurt we can disguise". The most telling line is about arithmetic: "In our route there wasn't you and me". Two travelers, no shared road.

Through the deep-sociality lens: a relationship is a third thing that exists between two people, and it can quietly stop existing. What remains is that "the silence screams too loud".

Still, the song's questions are collective. "Are we to blame for losing our light?" "Could it be true, have we become monsters?" It is not "you" or "I", it is "we". Even while ending, the song grieves the shared thing.

Our reading only. Track 09 on Roadburn Chronicles. Stream it on Spotify (link in bio).

What is the quietest way a relationship ever ended for you?

analyses.corpo: An Old Van and a Couple of Beers celebrates the open road, then admits "Lonely nights" and "Echoes of my travels past". A reading: freedom is better shared, "Laughing through hundred miles", and even the road becomes company: "Side by side with the road".
analyses.caption:
Freedom is better with company.

An Old Van and a Couple of Beers sounds like pure road-trip joy: "Open road", "Empty lanes", "no place I have to be". Look closer and the song keeps circling company: "Laughing through hundred miles with no fears". And when night falls: "Lonely nights", "Echoes of my travels past".

Deep sociality here is not an argument against solitude. The singer is "feeling small but feeling free" under a sky so vast, yet asking "Hold my dreams as the night turns into day". By the end the road itself is the companion: "Side by side with the road, I'll find my way".

Our reading of the lyrics. Track 10 on Roadburn Chronicles. Stream it on Spotify (link in bio).

Who is in your van?
